Belgium is facing a day of political turmoil on Monday as a national strike against planned austerity measures causes widespread disruption, with the government's future hanging in the balance.

Prime Minister Bart De Wever is to report to King Philippe, the third time in a month, on progress in agreeing a new cost-cutting budget with his coalition partners, as thousands march in Brussels against the same spending plans.

A national strike called by the country's main unions has grounded all flights, after air traffic controller Skeyes said it was unable to provide regular services at Belgian airports due to staff walking out.

Public transport, schools and other public services were also facing disruptions.

Belgium has seen repeated rounds of strikes and cost-of-living protests in recent months.

Much of the anger has been directed at De Wever's efforts to save €10 billion over the next few years in a bid to reduce the country's high deficit.

The issue has caused controversy also within the Flemish conservative's ruling coalition, which has been locked in budget talks for weeks.

De Wever offered his resignation to the king on 2 November over the budget impasse, but the monarch refused to accept it and gave him more time to find a solution.

To bring down the deficit, which exceeds 5% of GDP, the government is looking at spending cuts notably in healthcare and a VAT increase.`

Under the current fiscal framework, EU governments must keep their budget deficits below 3% of GDP and public debt under 60% of GDP.

But divisions within the coalition remain with the only leftist party in the mix, as well as unions pushing for taxes on high earners to offset some of the cuts.

It's all about the people, according to Joan Matabosch, artistic director of Madrid's Teatro Real. Budgets and political pressure

The EU investigation could lead to sweeping tariffs or quotas on materials used in defence, renewable energy and transport, as Brussels steps up efforts to protect European industry from cheap Chinese imports.

The European Commission launched an investigation on Monday into a surge in cheap imports of composite resins and glass fibre materials, primarily from China, amid growing concerns about the impact on European industry.

The materials are widely used in renewable energy, electricity infrastructure, transport, aerospace and defence.

The probe comes as the EU grapples with a flood of low-cost Chinese imports, which have risen by 25% over the past year, and seeks to rebalance its trade relationship with Beijing. The bloc's trade deficit with China has reached a record €1 billion a day.

The investigation is expected to last between nine and 11 months and could lead to quotas or tariffs on composite materials entering the EU.

Although China is the main target, the so-called "safeguard" measures would apply to imports from all the EU's trading partners.

The Commission opted for the broader investigation after imposing additional duties on resins and glass fibre reinforcements in recent years. Chinese producers were found to be circumventing these measures by shifting production to other countries, prompting European manufacturers to demand tougher protection.

“The Commission’s decision to launch this investigation confirms the seriousness of the situation facing Europe’s composite input materials industries,” said Ludovic Piraux, president of Glass Fibre Europe, which represents the EU's glass fibre industry.

“This case is about safeguarding the industrial capabilities we need to reduce our energy dependencies, strengthen our defence, transform mobility and remain a force in advanced manufacturing.”

EU countries back car deal

The investigation had been delayed for several months as the Commission pursued bilateral negotiations with Beijing to curb Chinese imports.

Those talks produced an agreement in October, although it covers only hybrid cars. Under the deal, the EU will introduce country-specific quotas allowing 350,000 Chinese hybrid vehicles onto the European market annually over four years, with a fixed annual adjustment rate of 6%.

EU officials expect the measures to more than halve current Chinese hybrid car exports to the bloc.

EU countries backed the agreement on Friday, clearing the way for it to take effect on December 1.

But the deal has done little to ease wider concerns about the impact of cheap Chinese imports on European industry, with growing calls for a more comprehensive approach to trade relations with Beijing.

The Commission hopes to extend negotiations to other sectors. EU Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič is expected to hold a video call with his Chinese counterpart, Wang Wentao, in January, ahead of a meeting in March 2027.

Antimicrobial resistance is a health security threat. Europe can lead global action

Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a global threat that no country can tackle alone.¹ World AMR Awareness Week, from 18 to 24 November, puts this shared responsibility into focus: countries must work together to preserve effective medicines and support the development of new treatments.

AMR raises the risk of serious complications and death from common infections. It is already putting pressure on health systems across the world.¹ Europe can play a key role in the global response to this issue, but only if the European Union (EU) and national governments implement effective support and rewards for antimicrobial innovation alongside existing stewardship policies. This article draws on discussions at a GSK-hosted educational AMR workshop at the European Society of Clinical Microbiology and Infectious Diseases (ESCMID) conference earlier this year and includes expert insights from:

· Florian Wagenlehner, Director, Clinic of Urology, Paediatric Urology and Andrology, Justus Liebig University, Giessen, Germany

· Jorge Mestre-Ferrandiz, Associate Professor, Charles III University of Madrid, Spain

· Matteo Bassetti, Director, Infectious Diseases Unit, AOM – IRCCS San Martino Polyclinic Hospital and Department of Health Sciences (DISSAL), University of Genoa, Italy

AMR is not tomorrow’s problem

AMR occurs when microbes, including bacteria and fungi, evolve to resist medicines designed to treat them, known as antimicrobials.¹ Globally, it is directly responsible for more than one million deaths each year and roughly €61 billion in direct healthcare costs.¹ ′ ² In Europe alone, the annual toll exceeds 35,000 lives and costs health systems around €11.7 billion.³ ′ ⁴

Europe is not on track to meet four of the five AMR targets set by the EU Council for 2030.⁵ These include ambitions to reduce overall antibiotic use, increase the proportion of prescribed antibiotics made up of first-choice “Access” antibiotics, and cut bloodstream infections caused by three major resistant bacteria.⁵ Failure to meet these targets will make it harder to reach the United Nations’ goal of reducing global AMR-related deaths by 10% by the same year.⁶ Without intervention, the burden of AMR on patients, healthcare systems and society will continue to grow.⁷

"For a patient, AMR becomes real when an antimicrobial does not work as expected," says Wagenlehner. "That can mean more complex treatment, more uncertainty and more time before we get the infection under control. When effective treatment options are limited or delayed, resistant infections can become life-threatening."

Responsible use matters – but new medicines are also needed

Misuse and overuse of antimicrobials remain the main drivers of AMR.¹ The more frequently microbes are exposed to antimicrobials, the greater the likelihood that resistance will develop.¹ This is why stewardship policies and practices that promote the careful and appropriate use of antimicrobials to slow down resistance are essential.

"Stewardship balances providing patients with the antimicrobials they need, while avoiding unnecessary use that would drive resistance," Wagenlehner explains. "For example, antibiotics are one type of anti-infective. They treat bacterial infections, not others such as viral ones, and using them when they are not needed can drive resistance."

However, stewardship alone is not enough. Europe also needs new antimicrobial options if it is to stay ahead of evolving resistance. These priorities are complementary; effective stewardship preserves today’s medicines, while innovation ensures we continue to stay ahead of resistance.

Why are we not getting enough new treatment options?

Since 2017, 17 new antimicrobials have been authorised globally, with only two of these representing new classes of antimicrobials.⁸ This means few new and differentiated treatments are coming forward.⁸ ′ ⁹ Innovation is therefore not keeping pace with the rise in drug resistance observed in microbes that cause infections, and we are not sufficiently addressing the diversity of ways in which microbes continue to outsmart the treatments that we have today.⁵

"When an infection becomes resistant to an antimicrobial, we need new medicines with diverse ways of overcoming that resistance," says Bassetti.

One of the main reasons resistance continues to outpace innovation is the increasingly challenging economics of antimicrobial research and development (R&D), exacerbated by ineffective funding models for antimicrobials once they become available.¹⁰ ′ ¹¹

The combination of high R&D costs and strong, appropriate stewardship creates a financial barrier to investment in innovative antimicrobials.¹⁰ ′ ¹¹ Traditional pharmaceutical business models rely on recouping R&D costs through sales volumes, yet novel antimicrobials are designed to be used sparingly to slow the development of resistance, creating a fundamental mismatch.¹⁰ ′ ¹¹

"Unlike medicines for common diseases, new antimicrobials are often held in reserve or used as a last resort, so companies may never recoup their R&D costs," says Mestre-Ferrandiz. "That is why many developers have stepped back from antimicrobial research, and why new economic incentives are needed."

Alongside the financial disincentive, health technology assessments (HTA) – the formal process used by health authorities to evaluate the value and costeffectiveness of new medicines and inform pricing and reimbursement decisions¹² – often fail to capture the full societal value of antimicrobials.¹³ This includes the readiness and resilience they bring to health systems and can lead to them being undervalued.¹³

"Innovative antimicrobials offer the best chance of getting ahead of resistance, rather than relying on variations of existing medicines," says Mestre-Ferrandiz. "Part of the value of a new antimicrobial is knowing there are additional options to treat infections if they become resistant to existing treatments."

Today, fewer developers are investing in antimicrobial R&D, resulting in a smaller group of new antimicrobials currently being researched or developed, with too few and insufficiently diverse products reaching the market.⁸ ’ ¹¹ Without intervention, this trend will only continue.

A new way of valuing antimicrobials is emerging

Governments are increasingly recognising this market failure and introducing "pull incentives", mechanisms that reward developers for bringing antimicrobials to market.¹¹ Some models delink financial returns from sales volumes, incentivising successful innovation regardless of how much of a product is sold.¹¹ “Appropriately funded pull incentives that delink payment from volume (i.e., payments independent of sales volume) and HTA processes that comprehensively assess the true societal value of antimicrobials are likely to be the most effective,” argues Mestre-Ferrandiz.

The UK's subscription model is the clearest example; it pays a fixed fee linked to National Health Service (NHS) value rather than volume, explicitly supporting stewardship and predictable supply.¹⁴This makes an antimicrobial available for use in the country, even if clinicians use it sparingly. This is a global first,¹⁴ but other countries have followed suit; Sweden has piloted a partially delinked revenue-guarantee model that rewards companies for keeping antibiotics of particular medical value available and ready for delivery.¹⁵

"Rewarding availability and clinical and societal value, rather than utilisation, can provide the predictability developers need without creating pressure to oversell antimicrobials that should be used responsibly," says Mestre-Ferrandiz.

Elsewhere in Europe, other forms of pull incentives have been implemented. Italy has created a €100 million fund to support development of, and access to, new innovative antimicrobials,¹⁶ while Germany has introduced a “reserve” antibiotic pathway that exempts qualifying products from part of the standard benefit-assessment process.¹⁷

The EU has signalled its intention to coordinate region-wide policies in a similar direction.¹⁸ This is an important step to support countries across the region in creating sustainable environments for antimicrobial innovation.

"A few promising examples do not yet add up to a stable system," cautions Bassetti. "The issue now is scaling these to create a sustainable market for antimicrobials across Europe."

Fair share: why European coordination matters

There is growing consensus amongst experts: delinked, value-based national pull incentives should be funded at fair share levels, an approach where countries contribute funding in proportion to the size of their economies.¹⁹ In 2019, analysts estimated $310 million (US) in global annual revenue, per priority antibiotic, across 10 years would be needed to support continued antibiotic R&D, helping bring more new and more diverse antimicrobials to patients.¹⁹ Splitting the financial commitment in proportion to the national gross domestic products (GDPs) of G7 and EU27 countries, a “fair share” approach, would spread costs and stabilise the market.¹⁹ However, currently only the UK and Italy are likely to meet their fair share targets.¹⁹

"Fair share is ultimately about solving the collective action problem," says Bassetti. "Broad participation, proportionate to economic capacity, is how you build a durable global system that supports innovation, supply resilience and access."

Every country benefits from new antimicrobials, but if only a few establish sufficient incentives, it will not be enough to increase R&D investment and will limit new options coming onto the market.¹¹ ’ ¹⁹

The next steps for Europe

Europe has an opportunity to drive the AMR response by setting a clear direction to implement solutions at scale across countries. The EU has already made this a political priority,¹⁸ but real change will only be realised if this is accompanied by national action.

This is an opportunity for European finance and health ministers to come together and look at AMR as an imminent threat to health security and economic stability.²⁰ ’ ²¹ Appropriate pull incentives can respond to the distinctive economics of AMR: antimicrobials require substantial investment to develop but must be used sparingly to preserve their effectiveness.¹⁰ ’ ¹¹ By rewarding value and availability rather than sales volume, these incentives can help reverse declining investment in antimicrobial R&D and support the development of effective new treatments for patients now and in the future.¹¹

"Europe already has the policy tools, scientific base and some early country examples," says Mestre-Ferrandiz. "The challenge is turning those pieces into a system for sustained progress."

World AMR Awareness Week is an opportunity to turn awareness into coordinated action that rewards antimicrobial value, promotes stewardship and strengthens health security and resilience. With 2030 targets approaching, Europe needs cross-sector collaboration to urgently address the growing burden of AMR.⁶

Balendra Shah's first visit to a neighbouring country since becoming prime minister also brought agreements on a railway, a hydropower plant and fuel infrastructure.

India has offered Nepal a development cooperation package worth 240 billion Nepali rupees (€1.4 billion) to help it recover from the catastrophic floods that tore through the Himalayan country in August.

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi made the announcement in New Delhi, India, on Monday, standing alongside his Nepali counterpart Balendra Shah.

"We express our deep condolences for the loss of lives caused by the devastating floods in Nepal in August," Modi said.

"To support Nepal's reconstruction, and give fresh momentum to its long-term development, we announce a development cooperation package worth 240 billion Nepali rupees (€1.4 billion)," he added.

New Delhi did not immediately say what the package would include. Nepal estimates the total cost of reconstruction at €4.35 billion.

His call came a day after the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Türkiye, collapsed without a deal, when the EU and other countries rejected a final text that made no mention of fossil fuels.

A disaster on a vast scale

The 26 August disaster began with a chain of events high in the Himalayas. A glacial collapse sent large amounts of rock, ice and meltwater into valleys below, triggering powerful floods downstream.

Scientists studying satellite imagery said the collapse appears to have involved the failure of bedrock beneath a glacier in the Himalayan region. The rockfall was powerful enough to register as a magnitude 5.2 seismic event.

The resulting surge of water and debris entered rivers that flow through valleys in Tibet and Nepal, causing them to rise rapidly.

Floodwaters swept away homes, buildings, roads and bridges and carried mud and rocks downstream.

More than 1,400 people were killed and 5,000 left missing. In the days after the disaster, at least 900 workers were reported missing from 12 hydropower projects damaged by the floods.

The scale of the death toll overwhelmed morgues and forensic teams.

'Deal with future disasters'

Nepal, a largely rural nation of 30 million people, produces only a tiny share of global greenhouse gas emissions. Shah said the disaster showed the "imperative to address the challenges of climate change through collective action".

In October, the United Nations' climate loss and damage fund approved $20 million (€18.2m) for Nepal. That is the most a country can request in a single application, and it was the first money the fund had set aside for any nation.

"Our commitment will be to help affected families rebuild their lives, create new opportunities and further strengthen Nepal's capacity to deal with future disasters," Modi said.

Disinformation, cyberattacks and the geopolitical use of migration put Spain in the sights of foreign powers. Experts urge shielding key sectors and speeding a joint European response to election interference.

In recent months, and especially throughout 2026, Europe has experienced an unprecedented escalation of hybrid attacks that have moved beyond the purely digital sphere to disrupt everyday services and critical infrastructure.

According to investigative journalists and European cybersecurity agencies such as the European Union Agency for Cybersecurity (ENISA), in the last six months more than 50 physical incidents linked to foreign intelligence have been documented, in addition to thousands of cyberattacks.

Looking ahead to Spain's general elections on 29 November, which hybrid threats are causing most concern in these elections?

Carlos Galán Cordero, a professor at Nebrija University and an expert in hybrid threats, warns about disinformation.

"Spain is an attractive target for foreign powers. We know that Russia uses disinformation as its main tool, but there are other actors that resort to different tactics to influence elections or stir up the streets, provoking some kind of social unrest," he said.

The battle to influence the Spanish vote

Dealing with hybrid threats requires a response on several fronts. The most urgent task is to shield critical infrastructure and modernise IT systems in key sectors, from healthcare and food supply to electoral networks, backed up by greater intelligence sharing and rapid reaction teams at European level.

"There are many actors with a strong interest in seeing one candidate or another win," Galán Cordero says. Asked which countries or agents are seeking to disrupt the electoral process in Spain, he points to multiple foreign powers.

Although effective contingency plans are in place, as seen recently with a disinformation campaign detected by Maldita.es that had very limited impact and barely any reach, experts warn that there is no room for complacency, since these actors can update their methods in search of greater interference.

Europe's common strategy

The European Union has a common strategy that has been significantly tightened between 2024 and 2026 in response to the surge in sabotage, cyberattacks and electoral interference.

However, national security remains the responsibility of each member state, so the European model works more as a coordination network, a system of binding standards and information exchange than as a single agency.

Focusing only on Russia gives a skewed picture, since other countries operate in this arena through hybrid threats such as using the migration crisis to exert pressure.

"Migration can indeed be used as a means of creating instability," Galán Cordero continues.

Although the Spanish government maintains that there is no conclusive evidence to formally attribute the mass entry into Ceuta to Morocco, geopolitics experts point out that this is precisely how the so called "grey zone" works.

Pro-Moroccan networks coordinated during episodes such as the Ceuta crisis show how third powers exploit regional vulnerabilities to apply pressure without leaving an official trace.

"Not long ago someone sent me a meme showing Spain as a coveted and contested piece on the global chessboard, fought over by Washington, Beijing, Moscow, Rabat and Tel Aviv. The truth is that there is already a contingency plan under way that is detecting and neutralising these actions in time," Galán Cordero adds.

Brussels' legal and diplomatic arsenal

The European Union's joint response combines political action, infrastructure protection and digital control. To react quickly to hostile campaigns, Brussels has the Hybrid Toolbox (EU Hybrid Toolbox), which allows sanctions and joint responses to be coordinated, and the new Emergency Security Protocol proposed by Ursula von der Leyen in September 2026, inspired by Article 4 of NATO.

To protect critical infrastructure, the European framework already imposes specific obligations. Internally, the NIS2 and CER directives require strict cybersecurity and early warning standards in vital sectors such as energy, healthcare and food.

In the digital and electoral sphere, the Digital Services Act (DSA) and the European Democracy Shield monitor algorithm transparency and advertising on platforms such as TikTok or X.

All this is reinforced through cooperation with NATO, based on joint exercises and the Helsinki Centre of Excellence for Countering Hybrid Threats.

When hybrid threats hit everyday life

It is also crucial to protect the information space by forcing digital platforms to provide genuine transparency about their algorithms and political funding, while strengthening media literacy among citizens so that disinformation become less effective.

The hybrid offensive in Europe is no longer an abstract threat; it is hitting everyday life and essential services head on.

In recent weeks the continent has seen a chain of incidents ranging from fake bomb threats on commercial flights and in schools to sophisticated digital sabotage against critical infrastructure, such as the cyberattacks suffered by several blood banks, which put at risk the preservation of vital reserves for transfusions and clinical trials.

This gap between technological speed and institutional response capacity defines today's information ecosystem.

In his book "La guerra: teoría para comprender los conflictos del siglo XXI" (War: A Theory for Understanding 21st-Century Conflicts) Spanish military officer Federico Aznar, an expert in disinformation and geopolitics, warns that "old solutions no longer work," and the new ones do not quite match the problems they are meant to address. That questioning of the current model is what underlies the idea of post truth."

Cybersecurity and monitoring to counter electoral falsehoods

With Spain's 29 November elections approaching, preventive measures combine the national security architecture with European cooperation, focusing on several key areas.

With the ballot in sight, Spain has activated its own preventive shield in line with Brussels. Under the coordination of the National Security Department and the Interior Ministry, bodies such as the National Cryptology Centre (CCN CERT) and INCIBE are working to secure the IT infrastructure of the electoral process, from data transmission networks to public information portals, against possible cyberattacks or impersonation attempts.

The digital investigation collective Antibot4Navalny, which tracks pro Russian disinformation campaigns, uncovered in November 2026 a coordinated offensive called Operation Matrioska, aimed at interfering in Spain's general elections.

The content pushed by this network seeks to discourage voting by alleging a supposed economic collapse caused by the housing crisis, calls for an end to sanctions on Russia and the withdrawal of funds from Ukraine, and promotes territorial fragmentation in Europe. The campaign circulates fake videos that mimic the look and style of media such as 'El País' and 'El Mundo' to lend credibility to disinformation narratives.

Fact checkers and citizens against electoral disinformation

The Monitor Disinfo association is dedicated to investigating, analysing and educating about disinformation and hybrid warfare. Carlos Galán Cordero is part of this association: "We analyse messages and campaigns on social media and share these issues with platforms such as Maldita.es, Newtral and similar organisations so that they can verify them."

Newtral has launched the FIMI Radar (Information Manipulation and Foreign Interference) to monitor foreign interference during the election campaign, while Maldita.es has highlighted its "Buloteca" archive ahead of 29N with the slogan 'Estas elecciones, la desinformación la frenamos juntos' - 'In these elections, we stop disinformation together'.

"This community is really good at helping to verify whether something is true or not," Galán Cordero continues. To stop these campaigns, he places the first line of defence with citizens, urging them to spot falsehoods and report them to the platforms themselves. Although there is a European legal framework to support this, such as the Digital Services Act (DSA), he warns that it will be in force for the 29N elections without yet having been rolled out with all the necessary effectiveness.

At the same time, intelligence services are keeping the digital ecosystem under surveillance to detect coordinated bot campaigns or narratives designed to sow doubts about the integrity of postal voting and the vote count.

Democratic resilience in the face of hybrid warfare and AI

This national deployment also draws on the European framework of the Digital Services Act (DSA), through which Spanish and EU authorities are demanding that platforms such as TikTok, X and Meta exercise greater control over their algorithms and political advertising during the final stretch of the campaign.

The aim is to prevent the scenario already seen elsewhere in Europe from being repeated in Spain: a combination of digital noise, falsehoods and sabotage designed to erode citizens' trust at the most sensitive moment for democracy.

Technological foresight and alliances to shield democracy

In this constantly evolving context, defending democracies means combining technological foresight with international cooperation. Professor Galán Cordero sums up the scale of the challenge like this: "Hostile actors have a lot of imagination when it comes to cyberattacks and are prepared to do whatever it takes to undermine the democratic values of Spain and Europe."

Facing campaigns increasingly driven by artificial intelligence, the expert highlights the preventive work of the National Cryptology Centre, which anticipates risks through constant simulations and testing, and stresses the need to act as part of a network: "We live in an increasingly globalised world and we need help from third countries to fight these threats. Spain is also an intelligence provider for allies that draw on our knowledge to tackle their own challenges."

In the face of a disinformation machine operating on an industrial scale through bot networks, troll farms and algorithms designed to fragment society, the response must be proactive.

Federico Aznar argues in his book that "technology reaches geopolitics" and that, in the era of post truth, "the main value to protect against these attacks is encapsulated in the integrity of society."

Armenia's prime minister announces electrical interconnections with Turkey and Azerbaijan, while Nvidia’s Rev Lebaredian warns of AI’s rising energy needs.

Just three years ago, Armenia and Azerbaijan were in the shadow of yet another bloody conflict. Today they are planning an electricity interconnection, with Turkey also in the picture.

Armenia has arrived on the global artificial intelligence (AI) map. And to keep its place, it needs electricity, partnerships and open borders.

Speaking at DigiTec 2026 in Yerevan, Armenia's prime minister Nikol Pashinyan announced that the country plans to connect its power grid with those of its two neighbours, Azerbaijan and Turkey.

He made the statement during a public discussion with Rev Lebaredian, vice president of Nvidia responsible for physical AI simulation.

"We will connect our grids with the electricity grids of Turkey and Azerbaijan. We are already connected with Iran and Georgia, and we are investing to make energy transmission more efficient," Pashinyan said.

He went on to announce that on Sunday, 22 November, the official launch will take place of TRIPP, the "Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity" project, stressing that "a very important part of this initiative is energy and the transit of electricity".

"This is truly a very significant and incredible transformation," Pashinyan said. "The 'Crossroads of Peace' project is becoming reality."

From energy surplus to AI demand

The rapid growth of AI factories is sharply increasing Armenia's demand for electricity; Firebird alone plans infrastructure with a capacity of 300 megawatts by the end of 2027.

At DigiTec, Pashinyan revealed that eight months ago the country had surplus electricity capacity, whereas now the expansion of data centres is creating the need to look for import suppliers.

Nvidia vice president Rev Lebaredian also underlined the need for more energy:

"How do we use our advantage now so that we can move from hundreds of megawatts to many gigawatts?" he asked the Armenian prime minister.

He noted that the country's current lead will not last forever; securing energy from more sources is critical if it is to make the most of it before other countries develop similar capabilities, he warned.

Lebaredian also linked energy interconnections to the prospect of lasting peace: by buying energy and providing AI services to its neighbours, Armenia can create mutual interests.

"We become important to each other and that will increase the chances of having peace that will last for a long time," he argued.

More sources, more options

Pashinyan outlined a mix of measures: developing renewable sources, particularly solar, creating storage and improving energy efficiency in buildings and businesses.

He also reiterated the intention to build a new nuclear power plant. The international interconnections form part of this broader effort at diversification.

According to Armenian news agency ARKA, Armenia and Turkey have already discussed restoring and activating the existing but inactive Gyumri-Kars power line.

"If Europe and the US do not build, they will import AI"

Armenia's determination to secure more computing power comes at a time when, in the US and in Europe, the expansion of data centres is provoking resistance over electricity supply, water use and the impact on local communities.

In an interview with Euronews, Lebaredian argued that much of this backlash reflects broader fears about AI and the way it is presented in public debate.

"I believe it is essentially a failure of leadership to describe in a positive way the future that AI will bring," he said.

In his view, the data centre becomes a target because it is "the physical manifestation of AI".

"When people are told that this will take their jobs or will kill them, of course they will not want it," he said.

When the infrastructure is in their area, he added, they can go to the local government and say "I don't want it".

Asked about resource requirements, he acknowledged the need for more energy: "The more energy you have, the more AI you can produce."

He backed further development of sustainable sources, adding that "there is also nuclear energy, which we should be using much more".

On water use, he pointed to the option of closed-loop cooling systems, acknowledging that different technologies involve trade-offs between water consumption, energy use and cost.

"You can use different cooling systems, but the cost may go up because you need more energy for cooling. Evaporative cooling can be more energy-efficient," he explained. "In some places there is a surplus of water. It all depends on local conditions."

On noise, he noted that data centres can be located in sparsely populated areas. "The facility is here, in Hrazdan. No one complains about noise and such issues," he said, referring to Firebird's AI factory.

At the same time, he warned that delaying the development of infrastructure could create new dependencies for Western economies:

"If the US and Europe do not develop their own supply, they will simply have to import AI from the places that are developing it," he stressed.

Many women work through their periods despite severe pain. One restaurateur from the Allgäu exempts affected female staff from duty. But how much consideration is appropriate at work?

When orders pile up in a restaurant, there is little time to catch your breath. For female employees with severe period pain, long hours on their feet, carrying heavy plates and working under time pressure in the kitchen and in service can be particularly hard.

At the Schlosskeller restaurant in Bad Hindelang in Bavaria they are not supposed to have to battle through their shift at any price. According to his own account, owner Peter Brutscher plans around their complaints when drawing up the rota.

On Instagram the restaurateur writes that for years he has deliberately taken female employees with severe period pain off the rota for two to four days, completely "without discussion".

Cramps, nausea or circulatory problems are physical limitations which, especially in the demanding hospitality sector, need to be taken seriously. His principle is: "The female cycle should not be ignored, but understood".

Not everyone has been understanding about this. "Of course I have been laughed at for it," Brutscher told the Allgäuer Zeitung. According to its report, his experience with one colleague prompted him to pay closer attention to such complaints when planning shifts.

How this consideration is organised is crucial, however. The magazine Focus reports that female employees can move shifts to another week. This does not automatically mean additional paid days off.

Many women work despite severe complaints

The fact that Brutscher is addressing a widespread problem is shown in a new study by the Institute for Employment Research (IAB), the research body of the Federal Employment Agency based in Nuremberg.

According to the study, 63% of the women surveyed feel limited in their daily work tasks by menstruation-related complaints, and 23% feel strongly limited.

For the study, a total of 2,107 women in dependent employment between 25-55 years of age were surveyed in spring 2026. They had all had their period in the previous six months.

According to the IAB, the weighted survey provides the first representative data on this topic for Germany.

The extent of the burden can hardly be read from days of absence alone. Only 13% had missed at least one full working day in the six-month period because of their complaints. Even among women who felt strongly impaired, 56% had no days off sick. Many therefore keep working even though they find their day-to-day tasks difficult.

In research this phenomenon is called presenteeism, which can go hand in hand with reduced concentration, resilience and productivity.

Menstruation still a taboo

There is also the concern about being perceived differently at work. More than 80% of respondents reject the idea that women should hide menstrual complaints in the workplace. At the same time, 64% report doing exactly that. More than half believe women would be seen as less resilient if they spoke about it openly.

Flexible working hours, longer breaks or working from home can ease the burden for those affected, but these options are not available to everyone. According to the IAB survey, 45% can arrange their working hours flexibly, and 37% can work from home.

Women with severe complaints in particular often make use of these possibilities, provided their job offers them.

Working from home is not an option in kitchens and front-of-house service. Other forms of relief can help here, such as more flexible shifts. Similar approaches exist in care work: RTL Nord recently reported on the concept of the intensive care service "Kunterbunte Butterfliege" in Grasberg, Lower Saxony.

The organisation takes account of the cycle and complaints of its female employees if they wish. Such models require staff to be able to express their needs and for work to be organised dynamically within the team.

Researchers recommend more flexibility

Menstrual complaints should also be taken more into account when designing working conditions. This is the view of a team led by Eva Schultz from the Institute of Occupational, Social and Environmental Medicine at Goethe University Frankfurt. In their review "The influence of the menstrual cycle on everyday working life" the authors summarised the existing research.

They describe how cramps, back and headaches, fatigue or difficulty concentrating can impair work. Tabooing the subject and a lack of flexibility in the workplace make the situation even more difficult.

As possible forms of support, the team mentions flexible working hours, working from home and more education in the workplace. At the same time, the authors call for caution when assessing the existing research. Many findings are based on retrospective information from the women surveyed, without their complaints being checked by a doctor.

Which measures are particularly effective therefore still needs to be investigated.

Spain as a pioneer

While Brutscher relies on arrangements within the business, Spain has created special legal protection. Since 1 June 2023, women there can obtain a special sick note for menstrual complaints that make them unable to work. This requires a medical certificate, and the state covers the financial security. The common term "menstruation leave" is therefore misleading. What is meant is health-related absence, not extra days off for rest.

Portugal has since followed with a more narrowly defined rule. Since April 2025, employees with severe menstrual pain as a result of doctor-confirmed endometriosis or adenomyosis can take up to three consecutive days of paid leave per month.

Now Spain is even extending its approach to certain conditions associated with the menopause. From 1 December 2026, affected employees will be able to obtain a special sick note if a medically diagnosed condition temporarily makes it impossible for them to work. The menopause alone does not create an entitlement.

Consideration must not become a disadvantage

A statutory special rule and flexible rota planning like Brutscher’s in the Oberallgäu are different ways of dealing with health burdens.

A voluntary shift swap is not a substitute for a sick note. In Germany, the general rules on illness apply to incapacity for work due to menstrual complaints.

The question is therefore not only what kind of support a company offers, but also how naturally employees can use it. The IAB survey illustrates the obstacle: more than half of women fear that an open approach to menstrual complaints will be taken as a sign of lower resilience.

In his restaurant, Brutscher relies on explicitly acknowledging such complaints. But for an offer like this to really provide relief, trust is crucial above all. Those who accept support should not have to fear for their professional reputation.

With a new computing power centre, international collaborations and a robotics lab, the small South Caucasus country seeks to turn its technological talent into greater economic influence.

The ancient Silk Road carried goods, knowledge and ideas between East and West. In Armenia, tech industry leaders are re-imagining it in the modern day: a network linking countries through the infrastructure needed to develop artificial intelligence.

"What we are starting to rebuild is the ancient Silk Road," said Rev Lebaredian, vice president of NVIDIA responsible for physical AI simulation, speaking at the DigiTec Technology Conference in Yerevan. "It is coming back, but in this new form, as a kind of AI Silk Road," he said.

He argued that Armenia and Kazakhstan can become its main pillars, with countries in the region contributing at different levels of the AI economy: energy, microprocessors, computing infrastructure, models and applications.

The vision goes beyond constructing data centres. It is about connecting markets, researchers, businesses and capital across borders, and creating a role for smaller economies in an industry dominated by much larger powers.

"We must work hard to create as much interdependence between us as possible," Lebaredian said. "That will help everyone’s prosperity and strengthen our security."

The emerging corridor is starting to take physical shape.

Firebird, a US-based AI infrastructure company with Armenian co-founders, opened a computing centre in Armenia in August and is building another one in Kazakhstan.

With more than 6,100 NVIDIA Blackwell processors, the Armenian facility provides the computing power businesses need to train and run artificial intelligence systems. NVIDIA itself is among its clients, while Perplexity also collaborates with it, linking the small country with international AI players.

A small country looking beyond its borders

This ambition runs through the DigiTec Conference, held from 20 to 22 November at Yerevan’s Meridian Expo Center. The organisers announced 125 speakers, including representatives of NVIDIA, OpenAI, Dell Technologies and Mozilla, bringing international technology companies together with governments and entrepreneurs from the region.

For Armenia’s technology community, the event is also a space to showcase the position the country wants to secure.

"We are creating a live platform" that brings together governments, investors and businesses from Europe, the Gulf, Central Asia and North America so they can develop technology, invest and expand their activities."

For a country of around three million people, these connections are essential. Armenia’s domestic market cannot by itself support the growth of an AI industry.

7% of national GDP

The political interest is also clear: the DigiTec programme includes a discussion between Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan and Nvidia's Lebaredian on turning the vision of an AI hub into reality.

The country is building on an already developed technology sector.

"The dream of building a technologically advanced Armenia pushed me to found the company and move from academic research into entrepreneurship," said Minasyan.

"It pushed my co-founder David to come back from Silicon Valley and start the company. It pushed many researchers from leading universities to come to Armenia and join forces to build here," he added.

This international network is a key element of the strategy. The Armenian diaspora provides connections through which know-how, information and business opportunities can flow.

The advice to build a supercomputer

"We knew we had the talent. We just had to convince the rest of the world that this is the right place to build and grow," he said.

For Lebaredian, computing infrastructure is the starting point for the next step, "physical artificial intelligence" that involves robots, autonomous vehicles and systems that operate in the real world after being trained and tested in simulations.

He sees applications from agriculture and manufacturing to health and transport, sectors that account for a large part of the global economy.

In Armenia, a new robotics and physical intelligence lab links universities, the state and businesses to develop researchers and practical applications.

"To turn the whole country into our laboratory and our industries into a lab," he proposed, referring to mines, agriculture and high-tech production such as drones.

In his view, Armenia’s small size can make cooperation easier and speed up the move from research to deployment.

That is where the success of the new Silk Road will be decided: in the country’s ability to turn computing power into home-grown businesses and technologies.

Does the EU need to invest more in data centres? To become a key player in artificial intelligence, it needs a lot more computing infrastructure to get there.

The European Union’s latest move is the AI Gigafactories initiative, which could mobilise over €30 billion in public and private investment to build large AI computing facilities.

The need is growing. The bloc had around 2,269 data centres in 2025, less than half the US total of 5,427. It also had around 12.4 gigawatts of data-centre capacity, almost 3 GW below estimated demand.

Data centres are buildings filled with servers that store and process information behind everyday services, from online banking and hospitals to public transport and streaming. Having them closer to users can make digital services faster and more reliable, while making it easier to comply with European privacy laws.

Data centres also attract major investment in Europe's digital infrastructure and create short- and medium-term jobs.

But there is a catch. Data centres consume huge amounts of electricity, water and land. In Ireland, they accounted for 23% of metered electricity consumption in 2025, up from 5% in 2015. Some regions now restrict new connections because their grids cannot keep up. Cooling servers also requires water, particularly problematic in drought-prone areas.

Then there is the cost. In 2025, average industrial electricity prices in the EU were roughly twice those in the US, making European facilities more expensive to operate. Building them also requires land, power lines, fibre-optic cables and expensive cooling systems.

Unless electricity comes from low-carbon sources, expanding data centres can increase emissions. The challenge is finding enough energy, space and money to support growth without putting too much pressure on local communities and the environment.

As AI becomes increasingly embedded within travel, research weighs in on its potential, the challenges and whether travellers are willing to completely put their trust in the developing technology.

Could your holiday soon be planned, booked and managed by artificial intelligence (AI) agents and tools?

With the new technology increasingly finding its place in the travel industry, and becoming more sophisticated, more travellers are turning to it for advice. But questions remain about whether AI is able to meet the demand of growing expectations and how much travellers are willing to trust it.

Whether it’s a gap between the technology developing rapidly, yet being unable to impart accurate and complex information, or its development becoming pervasive, yet relegated to the background, to which extent are travellers willing to use it for planning?

Here’s what industry leaders and research predicts for AI and how it could influence the future of travel.

Amadeus: Why 2032 is seen as a ‘horizon year’

According to new research by Amadeus, 2032 will be a “horizon year” for the industry where AI will “transform travel”.

In its latest report, "The Intelligent Journey 2032", the global travel technology company explored, using scenarios, the uncertainties and challenges that may shape a model of travel futures.

Developed in collaboration with Stratforma, the research identified critical uncertainties that may lie ahead:

The great disconnect: In this scenario, travellers’ use of AI comes to a head when fragmented systems, geopolitics and physical-world failures “overwhelm” its capabilities – the technology is able to “handle travel inspiration and recommendations but still cannot reliably deliver complex travel”, Amadeus said.

As such, humans will still be the “frequent fallback” in instances where automation cannot coordinate the whole journey and for high-stakes events.

Balanced boundaries: Amadeus foresees AI becoming increasingly capable by 2032, yet, users will be “more deliberate” about when to use it.

“Technology moves into the background, removing unwanted friction while preserving the choice, discovery and human connection that make travel valuable,” the company said.

Despite becoming increasingly sophisticated and pervasive, Amadeus predicts that “digital separation” will become sought after in exchange for authenticity, privacy, serendipity and genuine human interaction.

Machine vs. machine: By 2032, travellers’ expectations are expected to rise amid the industry having successfully integrated AI at a systems level. Travellers will also believe they have the tools in place that will deliver on their expectations. However, disappointments won’t be seen as unavoidable and will instead be blamed on suppliers.

Further, as more decisions take place between machines, it will become more important to have transparency on how said decisions are reached.

Travellers served? The industry will also need to navigate showcasing the value of AI integration amid what Amadeus referred to as “widespread customer anxiety” about how the technology can provide services at an attractive price. As such, traveller adoption of the technology is likely to be “uneven and hesitant”.

Concerns, such as privacy, autonomy, fairness and accountability, will remain at the forefront of travellers minds, which the industry will have to create safeguards for.

IATA: Travellers using AI for planning

In its 2026 Global Passenger Survey, the International Air Transport Association (IATA) found that AI is becoming a more prominent tool for people’s travel plans.

With results based on more than 10,000 responses from 200 countries, 49% of travellers said they have used AI for their planning. This includes 21% who have used it to search for flights to a specific destination, while 19% say they used it to look for the cheapest flights. Lastly, 17% of respondents used it for their travel inspiration.

"People are using AI to plan their travel,” Nick Careen, Senior Vice President, Operations, Safety and Security at IATA, said. “It’s important for airlines not only to ensure their offerings show up in AI, but also to develop convenient links to convert an AI conversation into a real booking.”

Dnata: AI and the traveller experience

For the Group CEO of global aviation and travel services company dnata, AI has the potential to transform travel experiences.

Speaking to Euronews Travel at the 2026 Arabian Travel Market in Dubai, Nabil Sultan Al Murr said that the technology is already changing how holidays are planned and sold.

“I honestly think that AI and technology will bring in huge advantages in terms of improving the whole passenger experience and being able to put out the best offers and products,” he said.

TOURISE: AI use for inspiration, but not for decisions

The “Future Traveller” report by TOURISE and Euromonitor International, which looks into how changing priorities are reshaping global tourism, found that travellers are keen to use AI assistance, but remain independent when it comes to the final decision-making.

According to the report, 31% of travellers will use it for travel planning and booking in 2026. This is a trend especially pronounced among Millennial users, with 34% using it for travel planning and booking, compared to their Gen Z counterparts at 29%.

Meanwhile, 59% use AI for information or recommendations – a trend especially high among Gen X (65%) and Baby Boomers (67%), as well as Millennials (57%).

Beyond just a planning tool, the research also suggested that AI will shift to becoming a “travel companion”, with 64% of respondents surveyed in 2025 saying they would pay for an AI assistant to provide information during a trip.

Booking.com: Excitement alongside sceptic sentiment in Europe

Travellers aren’t so keen on relinquishing total control, however. In its Global AI Sentiment Report released in 2025, Booking.com found that only 12% of travellers would be comfortable having AI tools make decisions on its own. This highlights a “clear boundary when it comes to fully handing over control to automation”, Booking said.

Further, when it came to feelings of distrust towards the information generated by AI, North America ranked highest at 32%, followed by Europe and the Middle East at 29%.

The research drew on insights from 37,000 consumers across 33 markets. Despite the above scepticism, 86% of European and Middle Eastern respondents reported being excited by AI and its opportunities, while a further 74% were familiar with the technology and how it works.

Globally, however, 91% are excited about AI, yet just 6% “fully trust” it. Meanwhile, 10% feel “very uncomfortable” about the technology, “refusing to trust AI without human approval”.

That being said, 89% also said they want to use AI in their future travel plans – especially as more people (24%) found it to be a more trusted source in comparison to bloggers or social media influencers, at 19% and 14%, respectively.

“Generative AI represents one of the most significant technological shifts of our era, fundamentally reshaping how consumers engage with the world around them," said James Waters, Chief Business Officer at Booking.com.

Waters added that developments within the technology is also " raising the bar” for what they expect in terms of their evolving needs.

Aven Hospitality: Accuracy will decide who travellers trust

Ahead of the Phocuswright Conference held in November in Florida, industry leaders weighed in on how travellers will plan trips in 2027, and pointed to the importance of accuracy and the technology “proving itself” in instances where there are disruptions.

For Teresa Mackintosh, CEO at Aven Hospitality, which provides AI-powered hospitality software to properties, the technology hasn’t yet been able to bridge the gap between its systems and booking channel – putting hotels at a disadvantage.

“It's one thing for an AI assistant to recommend a hotel,” she said. “But quite another for it to find accurate rates and check availability in real time, then complete a booking.”

This sentiment was echoed by Kenneth Johansen, Chief Revenue Officer at Travelport, who added: “As AI takes on a greater role in trip planning, the quality and accuracy of information behind those recommendations will become increasingly important.”

On the other hand, in instances where travellers are struck by cancelled flights, missed connections and sudden changes of plans, rather than queuing at an airport desk or staying on hold for customer service, travellers will get answers in minutes from AI.

"In 2027, servicing will be where travellers truly feel the impact of AI," Niklas Andréen, Chief Commercial Officer, Airline Tech at Sabre Corporation, said.

“Travellers will have disruptions spotted, rebooking options presented and changes confirmed in minutes, often before they've even realised there's a problem. We'll see agents increasingly able to shop, book, rebook and service travel, turning AI from an inspiration tool into a meaningful new distribution and servicing layer for the industry.”

Good morning. Leo Cendrowicz here, bringing you the Monday newsletter. This week, we’re dealing with more bombing of Ukraine, and the metaphorical bombing of the COP31 climate talks in Turkey.

It will be the first package since the Commission established a dedicated sanctions office within its Secretariat-General to improve enforcement inside and outside the bloc. The office aims to bring together 50 to 60 staff from across the Commission.

The timing is hardly accidental. The proposal comes amid preparations for multilateral peace talks involving Russia, Ukraine, the US and Europe. Will Moscow seize on the sanctions as another excuse to reject the format? Don't rule it out.

The prevailing view in European capitals is that Russia has little interest in serious negotiations, and that more economic pressure is needed to change the equation.

Diplomacy meets reality. After last week's much-hyped summit between Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping, and the gathering of the Coalition of the Willing, there is precious little evidence of peace breaking out.

After two weeks of negotiations and a record 44 hours of overtime, COP31 ended in spectacular disarray on Sunday, with the EU leading a rebellion against a deal that threatened to take global climate policy backwards.

The showdown in Antalya, Turkey, came after oil-producing countries, led by Saudi Arabia, resisted even reaffirming the commitment made in Dubai three years ago to transition away from fossil fuels.

Ireland's Climate Minister Darragh O'Brien, speaking for the EU, refused to swallow the compromise. "We will not accept negotiating backwards in time," he declared, to applause. The UK, Norway and vulnerable island states joined the revolt.

The proposed pact also promoted controversial carbon capture technologies, while failing to guarantee that a new electrification target would be powered by clean energy.

Climate flop. The result? No overarching agreement, and the biggest failure of UN climate diplomacy since Copenhagen in 2009.

But Europe's targets will be harder to achieve without global cooperation, particularly as its industries complain about the costs of going green.

At the start of every hour, the street takes on silvery tones in response to its neighbour on the other bank of the Seine. For the next two months, the illuminations of the Champs-Élysées and the Eiffel Tower will sparkle in unison.

The year 2026 also marks the return of the Christmas market after 10 years away. Two hundred exhibitors are set up in wooden chalets between the Rond-Point des Champs-Élysées and Place de la Concorde.

The specifications stipulate fully organic flour, French meat and mulled wine, and a vegetarian option in every food chalet. "80% of what is on offer will be made in France," stressed Marc-Antoine Jamet, secretary general of LVMH and president of the Comité des Champs-Élysées, speaking to RMC. A Fabriqué à Paris label is even being introduced in the craft market.

A skating rink, a fairground ride, Santa's House, a monumental reindeer and around 20 scenographic installations complete the set-up.

Festive season in joy, but also in calm

The president of the Comité des Champs-Élysées points out that for shopkeepers on the most famous street in Paris, the illuminations and the Christmas market are a matter "of image, reputation, renown and attractiveness". Although the prefecture has so far not authorised Paris demonstrations to march up the capital's most famous avenue, the site is a symbolic location regularly used during social protest.

The Comité des Champs-Élysées is nonetheless showing optimism. It says it is in regular contact with the Paris prefect.

Tekever's funding round has decisively contributed to accelerating investment in Portugal, which is expected to grow 187% this year. The country is gaining ground in the European landscape, following the broader trend of recovery in technological investment in the rest of Europe.

Portugal's tech ecosystem is going through one of its most significant years in terms of attracting capital. Portugal is expected to reach 910 million dollars in venture capital investment in 2026, according to estimates in the State of European Tech 2026 (source in Portuguese) report, compiled by Atomico.

The amount represents growth of 187% compared with the 320 million dollars recorded in 2025. This trend places Portugal among the ten European countries with the highest volume of investment in technology companies, in tenth position, after finishing last year in 14th place.

One of the main factors behind this development is Tekever's financing operation. The Portuguese company, specialised in developing autonomous systems and artificial intelligence technologies, secured an investment round worth 580 million dollars in September 2026.

The scale of this transaction illustrates the growing interest among investors in domestic companies that are able to develop technology in strategic sectors, particularly defence.

Portugal's performance mirrors a broader trend of recovery in European technology investment. According to Atomico, the continent is expected to register 81 billion dollars in investment during 2026, equivalent to growth of 62% compared with the previous year. It will be the second-best result ever, only behind the 94 billion dollars reached in 2021.

Although technology investment in Europe is rising, capital is becoming concentrated in an ever smaller number of companies. Since 2021, the number of early funding rounds (first-money-in, before Series A) has been declining, with a drop of almost 30% between 2021 and 2025. Over the same period, the combined number of Series A and Series B rounds fell by 19%.

The data for 2026, which include an extrapolation to estimate the full-year results, point to further declines, according to the report.

Technology sector consolidates its role as a driver of employment

Europe is also expected to reach a record of 40,000 new technology founders in 2026, 36% more than in 2025 and 80% more than in 2024. In 2026, 29% of the world's new founders of technology companies were based in Europe, the largest share of any region, slightly ahead of the United States, with 28%.

The overall value of Europe's technology ecosystem has likewise grown every year since 2017, with the sole exception of 2022. It is currently valued at 4.4 trillion dollars.

Over the past decade, technology has been Europe's biggest engine of job creation, generating around 6% more jobs each year.

This makes the sector the fastest-growing in terms of job creation, outpacing the traditional growth rate of industries such as healthcare, hospitality and construction, as well as jobs in sectors such as banking, insurance, consulting and accounting. Since 2016, technology jobs have grown by 62% overall, while non-technology jobs have risen by only 11%.

The vast majority (81%) of these roles are in local companies headquartered in Europe, according to Atomico's report.

US invested 5 times more in AI in nine months than Europe did in a decade

European investment in artificial intelligence and computing is growing at an unprecedented pace, having more than doubled in 2026 to 20 billion dollars, compared with 9.5 billion recorded the previous year.

Even so, Atomico points out that the gap with the United States has widened over the past three years. The increase in US investment over nine months this year alone exceeded all the capital Europe has put into this sector over the course of a decade.

A significant share of global funding is also concentrated in a small number of artificial intelligence companies, with OpenAI and Anthropic together capturing 61% of worldwide investment.

This difference, the report indicates, reflects not only the size of the US market but also its ability to mobilise capital for projects that require large-scale technology infrastructure, particularly computing capacity.

According to Atomico, European private capital markets still do not have sufficient depth to finance operations of this size. Faced with this reality, European companies, entrepreneurs and institutions are forced to make strategic choices about the areas in which they should invest and compete. The challenge is to develop funding sources capable of keeping pace with Europe's technological ambitions and allowing companies to grow on a global scale.
